tool.name: C#
tool.tagline: Modern, statically typed language for .NET: backends, desktop, games and cloud
tool.description: C# is Microsoft's statically typed, object-oriented language for the .NET platform, with strong functional features such as LINQ, lambdas, records and pattern matching. It is used for web backends with ASP.NET Core, Windows and cross-platform apps, Unity games and cloud services. Learning it gives you a productive, fast, well-tooled language with a huge standard library.

glossary.def: Microsoft's free platform for running C# programs: the runtime that runs them plus a large collection of ready-made code.
The free download for writing C# programs. It contains the C# compiler, the .NET runtime and the dotnet command.
The dotnet command you type in a terminal to create, build, run, test and publish C# projects.
The .csproj file that describes a C# project: what it builds, which .NET version it targets and which packages it uses.
C# statements written straight into Program.cs, without wrapping them in a class and a Main method; the compiler adds that wrapper for you.
In C#, a group of statements inside braces { }, such as the body of an if, a loop or a method.
A C# keyword that passes the caller's variable itself into a method, so the method can change it.
In C# pattern matching, a description of a shape a value may have, such as > 0, null or { Status: "paid" }, checked with is or switch.
To create a class that inherits from another; the new class is a derived class (a subclass).
A where rule on a C# generic type, such as where T : IComparable<T>, saying what T must support.
When a lambda uses a variable from the code around it, it captures that variable: it keeps access to the variable itself, even after that code has finished.
The value an extension method is called on: in "x".IsBlank(), the receiver is "x".
A .NET queue that one part of a program writes items into and another reads from, possibly at the same time.
C#'s lock statement: it lets only one thread at a time run a piece of code, so shared data isn't changed by two threads at once.
A part of an array, string or span picked out by position, such as items 2 to 4.
An optimization where the compiler copies a small method's code into the place that calls it, saving the cost of the call.
A compiler check of whether an object is ever used outside the method that creates it; if not, it needn't go on the heap.
A measurement of which lines of your code ran during the tests, showing the parts no test checks.
The number that identifies one location in the computer's memory; a pointer holds one.
A C# shortcut that puts constructor parameters right after the class name: class Account(string owner) { ... }.
A property with no stored value that works out its value each time it is read, like Age => Today.Year - BirthYear.
Square brackets listing items, like [1, 2, 3], used to fill an array or a list in C#.
A keyword such as public or private that says which other code may use a class or one of its members.
A field, property or method that belongs to the class itself rather than to any one object, like Math.Max.
A C# property written { get; set; }: the compiler creates the hidden field that stores its value.
Braces after new that set properties by name: new Person { Name = "Ada" }.
A C# compiler feature that tracks which variables may hold null (written string?) and warns before you use one without checking.
A line such as using System.Text; at the top of a C# file that lets you write that namespace's class names without the namespace in front.
A project setting that makes common .NET namespaces such as System available in every file without writing using lines.
What building one C# project produces: a .dll file or a program you can start, holding the compiled code.
.NET's online catalog of shared packages. dotnet add package downloads a package from it into your project.
A C# type whose data sits directly in the variable, such as int, bool or a struct. Copying the variable copies the data.
A C# type, such as a class, string or array, whose data lives in a separate object; variables hold only a reference to it, so copies share the object.
Wrapping a value such as an int inside a new object so it can be stored where any object is allowed. It costs time and memory.
Microsoft's framework for building websites and web services in C#.
A C# class or struct meant for holding data: the compiler writes its constructor and properties, and two records count as equal when their contents match.
C# syntax that copies a record while changing some properties: var older = p with { Age = 37 };
A C# expression that picks a result by checking a value against a list of patterns: x switch { 1 => "one", _ => "many" }.
One pattern => result line of a C# switch expression.
A C# type for variables that hold a method, so the method can be passed around and called later. Func and Action are the built-in ones.
Language Integrated Query: C# methods such as Where, Select and OrderBy that filter, transform and sort collections of data.
The .NET interface for any sequence of items you can loop over with foreach, such as arrays and lists. LINQ methods work on it.
.NET's main library for working with databases: you read and save rows as C# objects, and it writes the SQL for you.
A .NET object standing for work that will finish later, such as a download; Task<T> also carries the result. You wait for it with await.
The .NET interface for objects that hold something besides memory, like an open file; calling its Dispose method releases it right away.
using var x = ...; in C#: it makes sure x is released (its Dispose method called) when the surrounding block ends, even after an error.
A popular free library for writing and running tests in .NET; [Fact] and [Theory] mark test methods.
A static method that can be called as if it belonged to another type: "text".IsBlank() really calls TextExtensions.IsBlank("text").
A value passed into slow .NET operations so they can be asked to stop early, for example when a time limit passes.
Rules for when a generic type can stand in for the same type with a different item type, e.g. using an IEnumerable<string> where an IEnumerable<object> is expected.
Writing one C# method that does arithmetic on any number type (int, double, decimal...) using interfaces such as INumber<T>.
A .NET window onto part of an array, string or other memory that lets you read and slice it without copying.
A C# struct that may only live in a method's short-lived local storage, never inside an object, such as Span<T>.
Code that looks at types while the program runs: listing a class's properties, reading its attributes, or calling a method by its name.
An add-on to the C# compiler that reads your code while it builds and adds extra generated C# code to the program.
A .NET publish step that removes code the app never uses, making the output smaller.
Publishing a .NET app compiled fully to machine code ahead of time: one file that starts fast and needs no installed .NET.
An age group the .NET garbage collector sorts objects into (0, 1 or 2) so it can check young objects often and old ones rarely.
A separate memory area where .NET puts objects of 85,000 bytes or more, mostly big arrays; it is cleaned less often.
Intermediate language: the compact instructions the C# compiler produces. The .NET runtime turns them into the computer's own instructions while the program runs.
The .NET runtime first compiles each method quickly with few optimizations, then recompiles the most-used methods with full optimizations.
Profile-guided optimization: measuring how the program actually runs, then using those measurements to optimize the busiest code.
A .NET publish option that stores precompiled machine code in the assemblies so the app starts faster.
Platform Invoke: the .NET feature for calling functions in libraries written in C, such as the operating system's own functions.
Converting values between .NET's format and C's format when .NET code calls a C library, e.g. turning a string into C-style bytes.
C# code marked unsafe that may work with raw memory addresses (pointers); the compiler can no longer check it for memory mistakes.
Telling the .NET garbage collector not to move an object in memory, so a raw address to it stays valid.

concepts.name: Run C# with the dotnet CLI
concepts.summary: Install .NET, then create, build and run your first C# program by typing dotnet commands in a terminal.
concepts.why: Every C# program, from a tiny experiment to a large web service, is created and started with the same dotnet command, so this is where you begin.
concepts.body:
A **program** is a list of instructions for the computer. It is written in a **programming language**, such as C#: a precise, limited language that both people and computers can read. You type those instructions into an ordinary text file. That human-readable text is called **source code**, and C# source files end in `.cs`.

The computer can't follow C# text directly. A **compiler** first translates it into a compact form the computer can run; this step is called **compiling** (or building). When the program starts, the **runtime**, the engine that runs C# programs, carries out those instructions.

C# comes with **.NET**, Microsoft's free platform for C#: the runtime plus a big collection of ready-made code. To write programs, install the free **.NET SDK**. It contains the compiler, the runtime and a command called `dotnet`.

You use `dotnet` from a **terminal**: a window where you type commands instead of clicking (Terminal on macOS and Linux, Windows Terminal on Windows). Working by typing commands is called using the **command line**, and a program used that way is a **CLI** (command-line interface). So `dotnet` is often called the **dotnet CLI**.

- `dotnet new console -o Hello` creates a folder `Hello` with a starter program, `Program.cs`, and a **project file**, `Hello.csproj`, which describes how to build it.
- `cd Hello` switches the terminal into that folder.
- `dotnet run` compiles the project and starts it. `dotnet build` only compiles.

Each instruction in C# is a **statement**, and most statements end with a semicolon `;`. In `Program.cs` you simply write statements one after another, and they run from top to bottom. C# calls this style **top-level statements**. (Older examples wrap the same code in `class Program` and `static void Main`; you don't need that.)

`Console.WriteLine("Hello")` shows a line of text in the terminal; text inside double quotes is used exactly as written. `Console.ReadLine()` waits for the user to type a line and press Enter. Anything after `//` on a line is a comment: a note for humans that the compiler ignores.

Since .NET 10 you can even skip the project: `dotnet run app.cs` runs a single file, handy for quick experiments.
takeaways: The .NET SDK gives you the compiler, the runtime and the dotnet command
dotnet new creates a project; dotnet run compiles it and starts it
Statements in Program.cs run from top to bottom, and most end with ;
pitfalls: Typing dotnet run in the wrong folder: the terminal must be in the folder that holds the .csproj file.

quiz.q: What does dotnet run do in a project folder?
options: Packages the program so you can send it to other people
Compiles the project if needed and then starts it
quiz.explain: dotnet run builds the project when something changed and then launches the program.

quiz.q: What is the compiler's job?
options: Translating your C# source code into a form the computer can run
Typing commands into the terminal for you
quiz.explain: The compiler turns human-readable source code into something the .NET runtime can execute, and reports mistakes it finds.

concepts.name: Variables and built-in types
concepts.summary: Store values in named variables and learn C#'s basic types: whole numbers, decimals, true/false and text.
concepts.why: Every program keeps track of values, and picking the right type of value avoids rounding errors and numbers that silently wrap around.
concepts.body:
A **variable** is a name that holds a value so you can use it later, like a labelled jar. You create one by writing its type, a name and a starting value: `int count = 3;`. Later you can put a new value in it: `count = 4;`.

The **type** (or data type) says what kind of value the variable may hold: a whole number, a number with decimals, text, and so on. C# is **statically typed**: each variable's type is fixed when you write the code, and the compiler refuses to build a program that puts the wrong kind of value in it. The mistake shows up as a **compile error** before the program ever runs.

`var` lets the compiler work out the type from the starting value: `var price = 9.99m;` makes `price` a `decimal`. The type is still fixed; `var` only saves typing.

The types you'll use most:

- `int` for whole numbers (**integers**) such as `-3` or `42`, up to about two billion; `long` for bigger ones.
- `double` for numbers with decimals in measurements. It is a **floating-point number**: stored approximately, so `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`.
- `decimal` for money: it stores decimal digits exactly. Its values end in `m`, as in `9.99m`.
- `bool` for yes/no values, `true` or `false` (a **boolean**).
- `char` for one character in single quotes, `'a'`; `string` for text in double quotes, `"hello"`.

A value written straight into the code, like `42` or `"hello"`, is called a **literal**.

Arithmetic uses `+ - * /`, and `%` gives the remainder. Careful: dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number and throws away the remainder (**integer division**): `7 / 2` is `3`. Write `7 / 2.0` to get `3.5`. `==` asks "are these equal?" and gives a `bool`.

An `int` pushed past its largest value silently wraps around to a big negative number, so use `long` when values can get huge.

To turn text into a number, use `int.Parse("42")`. If the text might not be a number, such as something a user typed, use `int.TryParse(text, out var n)`: it gives `true` and puts the number in `n`, or gives `false` instead of crashing.
concepts.code:
int count = 3;
var price = 9.99m;                      // var: the compiler picks decimal
Console.WriteLine(count * price);       // 29.97
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2);               // 3   (whole-number division)
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2.0);             // 3.5
Console.WriteLine(7 % 2);               // 1   (the remainder)
Console.WriteLine(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3);    // False (double is approximate)
Console.WriteLine(0.1m + 0.2m == 0.3m); // True  (decimal is exact)

count = count + 1;                      // store a new value in count
Console.WriteLine(count);               // 4

int big = int.MaxValue;                 // the largest possible int
Console.WriteLine(big + 1);             // -2147483648 (wrapped around)

bool ok = int.TryParse("12x", out var n);
Console.WriteLine(ok);                  // False: "12x" is not a number
takeaways: A variable is a named value with a fixed type: `int x = 3;` or `var x = 3;`
int for whole numbers, decimal for money, double for measurements, bool for true/false, string for text
Dividing two ints throws away the remainder: 7 / 2 is 3
Use TryParse for text a user typed
pitfalls: Writing double x = 7 / 2; and expecting 3.5: both numbers are ints, so the division gives 3 before it is stored.

quiz.q: What is the value of 5 / 2 * 2.0 in C#?
quiz.explain: 5 / 2 is integer division giving 2, then 2 * 2.0 is the double 4.0.

quiz.q: Which type should hold a price like 19.99 in a shop program?
quiz.explain: decimal stores decimal digits exactly, so money adds up correctly; int has no decimals and double is approximate.

concepts.name: Strings and interpolation
concepts.summary: Work with text: join and format strings, use methods like Trim and Split, and pick out characters by position.
concepts.why: Almost every program builds or reads text, from messages on screen to file names and reports.
concepts.body:
A **string** is a piece of text, a sequence of characters such as `"Hello, Ada!"`. Programs build strings all the time: messages, file names, reports.

Values in C# come with built-in actions called **methods**. You use one by writing a dot, its name and parentheses: `name.ToUpper()` gives an upper-case version of `name`. Some methods need extra information inside the parentheses: `text.Replace("cat", "dog")`.

Strings are **immutable**: once made, a string never changes. `ToUpper`, `Replace` or `Trim` (which removes spaces at both ends) give back a **new** string, so keep the result: `name = name.Trim();`.

An **operator** is a sign, like `+`, that does something with values. On strings, `+` joins them end to end (**concatenation**): `"Hi, " + name`. Often clearer is **string interpolation**: put `$` before the quotes and write values inside braces, `$"Hi, {name}! You are {age}."`. After a colon you can add a format: `{total:N2}` shows two decimals with thousands separators.

Some characters need a short code inside quotes, called an **escape sequence**: `\n` starts a new line, `\"` is a quote mark, `\\` a backslash. A string that starts with `@` treats backslashes as ordinary characters, which suits Windows folder paths: `@"C:\temp\new"`. Text between three quote marks, `"""..."""`, may contain quote marks freely.

Other handy tools: `Length` (the number of characters), `Contains`, `StartsWith`, `IndexOf`, `Split` (cut into pieces) and `string.Join` (glue pieces together). Each character has a position number, its **index**, and counting starts at 0: `s[0]` is the first character, `s[^1]` the last, `s[..3]` the first three.

`==` compares the text of two strings. To ignore upper and lower case, use `string.Equals(a, b, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`.

Building a long text with many `+` steps makes a new string at every step. A `StringBuilder` collects the pieces and makes one string at the end with `ToString()`.
concepts.code:
string name = "  Ada  ".Trim();               // "Ada" (spaces removed)
decimal total = 1234.5m;
Console.WriteLine("Hi, " + name + "!");       // Hi, Ada!
Console.WriteLine($"Total: {total:N2}");      // Total: 1,234.50
Console.WriteLine(name.ToUpper());            // ADA
Console.WriteLine(name);                      // Ada (unchanged)
Console.WriteLine(name.Length);               // 3
Console.WriteLine(name[0]);                   // A  (index 0 is the first)
Console.WriteLine(name[^1]);                  // a  (the last character)
Console.WriteLine("Line 1\nLine 2");          // prints two lines
Console.WriteLine(@"C:\temp\new");            // C:\temp\new

string[] parts = "red,green,blue".Split(','); // three pieces of text
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" + ", parts)); // red + green + blue
Console.WriteLine("abc" == "ab" + "c");       // True

var sb = new System.Text.StringBuilder();     // new: see the classes lesson
sb.Append("a").Append("b").Append("c");
Console.WriteLine(sb.ToString());             // abc
takeaways: A string is text; methods like ToUpper return a new string and leave the old one as it was
$"Hi, {name}" puts values into text
Characters are numbered from 0: s[0] is the first
== compares the text of two strings
pitfalls: Calling s.Replace("a", "b") and ignoring the returned string: s itself doesn't change.

quiz.q: After string s = "hi"; s.ToUpper(); what is s?
quiz.explain: ToUpper returns a new string; s still holds the original "hi".

quiz.q: What text does $"{2 + 3} apples" produce?
quiz.explain: With $ in front, the expression inside the braces is calculated and its value is put into the text.

concepts.name: Conditions and loops
concepts.summary: Make your program choose between paths with if and switch, and repeat steps with for, foreach and while loops.
concepts.why: Real programs react to their input and repeat work; choosing and repeating are the two basic tools for both.
concepts.body:
So far each statement runs once, top to bottom. Two tools change that: choosing which code runs, and repeating code.

An **if statement** runs code only when a condition is true, like a recipe saying "if the dough is sticky, add flour". The condition goes in parentheses and must be a `bool`. The code to run goes in braces; statements grouped in braces like this form a **block**:

```csharp
if (age >= 18) { Console.WriteLine("adult"); }
else { Console.WriteLine("minor"); }
```

Conditions use comparison operators: `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. Combine conditions with `&&` (and), `||` (or) and `!` (not). Add more paths with `else if`. C# insists on a real `bool`, so `if (count)` is an error; write `if (count > 0)`.

A **switch statement** compares one value against a list of possible values and runs the code for the one that matches. Each case ends with `break`. Several labels can share one case, as in the weekend example below, and `default` handles everything else.

A **loop** repeats code. Each pass through it is called an **iteration**.

- `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)` counts: start `i` at 0, keep going while `i < 5`, and add 1 after each pass (`i++`).
- `foreach (var item in items)` visits each item of a group of values, such as a list of scores, in order.
- `while (condition) { ... }` repeats as long as the condition stays true. Something inside must eventually change it, or the loop never ends. `do { ... } while (condition);` is the same but always runs at least once.

Inside a loop, `break` stops the loop early and `continue` skips straight to the next iteration.

To choose between two values in one line, write `condition ? a : b`: `string label = age >= 18 ? "adult" : "minor";`.
takeaways: if runs code only when a bool condition is true; else if and else add other paths
for counts, foreach visits every item, while repeats until its condition turns false
break leaves a loop; continue jumps to the next iteration
Each switch case ends with break
pitfalls: Writing a while loop whose condition never becomes false, so the program never finishes.

quiz.q: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) run its body?
quiz.explain: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2; when i reaches 3 the condition i < 3 is false and the loop stops.

quiz.q: Why doesn't if (count) compile when count is an int?
options: if needs a bool condition, such as count > 0
count must be created with var
quiz.explain: C# never treats a number as true or false; the condition must be a bool.

concepts.name: Methods and parameters
concepts.summary: Wrap steps into reusable methods with parameters and return values, plus default values, named arguments and tuples.
concepts.why: Methods let you write a piece of logic once, give it a name and use it everywhere, which keeps programs short and readable.
concepts.body:
A **method** is a named, reusable piece of code: you write the steps once, give them a name, and run them whenever you need by **calling** the method. You already call methods like `Console.WriteLine`; now you write your own. Many other languages call these **functions**.

`static int Add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }` declares a method:

- `int` before the name is the return type: the kind of value the method hands back. `void` means it hands back nothing.
- `Add` is the name.
- `(int a, int b)` are its **parameters**: named inputs, each with a type.
- `return a + b;` ends the method and hands back the **return value**.

Calling `Add(2, 3)` passes the **arguments** 2 and 3 into `a` and `b` and runs the body; the call itself then stands for the value 5. `static` means the method can be called on its own (objects, the alternative, come in the classes lesson).

For a one-line method, `=>` replaces the braces and `return`: `static int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;`. In `Program.cs`, your methods can sit right among your statements.

Ways to make calls easier:

- A parameter can have a **default value**, used when the caller leaves it out: `string greeting = "Hello"`.
- **Named arguments** label the values at the call: `Greet("Ada", greeting: "Hi")`.
- `params int[] values` accepts any number of arguments: `Sum(1, 2, 3)`.

A method gets its own copy of each argument, so changing a parameter inside doesn't change the caller's variable. To let the method change it, mark both the parameter and the argument with **ref**: `Double(ref n)`. An `out` parameter hands back an extra result, as in `int.TryParse(text, out var n)`.

To hand back several values at once, return a **tuple**, a small group of values: `(int Min, int Max)`.

Several methods may share a name if their parameters differ; this is **overloading**. `Console.WriteLine` works with both text and numbers this way.
takeaways: A method is named, reusable code: parameters go in, a return value comes out
void methods return nothing; => writes a one-line method
Default values and named arguments keep calls readable
Arguments are copies; ref lets a method change the caller's variable
pitfalls: Ignoring the returned value: Add(2, 3); on a line by itself calculates 5 and throws it away.

quiz.q: static int Twice(int x) => x * 2; What does Twice(Twice(3)) return?
quiz.explain: The inner call gives 6, and Twice(6) gives 12.

quiz.q: In Greet("Ada", greeting: "Hi"), what is greeting: "Hi"?
options: A named argument for the greeting parameter
quiz.explain: A named argument labels which parameter a value is for, so you can skip or reorder optional ones.

concepts.name: Arrays and List<T>
concepts.summary: Keep many values together in fixed-size arrays or growable List<T>, read them by position, and loop over them.
concepts.why: Nearly every program works with groups of values, such as scores, names or orders, kept in arrays or lists.
concepts.body:
Often you need many values of the same kind: all the scores in a game, all the names on a guest list. Instead of one variable each, you keep them together.

An **array** holds a fixed number of values in order: `int[] scores = [72, 95, 40];`. The `[]` after the type means "array of". Each item has a position number, its **index**, counting from 0: `scores[0]` is 72 and `scores[2]` is 40. You can change an item with `scores[1] = 99;`, and `scores.Length` gives the number of items. An index that doesn't exist, like `scores[3]` here, stops the program with an error.

`new int[5]` makes an array of five zeros when you'll fill it in later.

An array can't grow. When you need to add and remove items, use a list: `List<string> names = ["Ada", "Linus"];`. The type in angle brackets says what kind of item the list holds. Lists offer methods such as:

- `Add(x)` puts an item at the end; `Insert(0, x)` at the front.
- `Remove(x)` removes an item; `RemoveAt(i)` removes the item at index `i`.
- `Contains(x)` checks whether an item is there; `Count` gives the size (lists say `Count`, arrays say `Length`).

Square brackets with items inside, `[1, 2, 3]`, are a **collection expression**; they work for arrays and lists alike. `..` copies in all the items of another collection: `[..first, ..second, 99]`.

`^1` counts from the end, so `names[^1]` is the last item. A range like `scores[1..3]` gives the items at index 1 and 2: the end number is not included.

One surprise: a variable holding a list doesn't hold the items themselves, only a **reference** to them, like a note saying where the list lives. `var other = names;` copies the note, not the list, so both variables reach the same items and adding through one shows up in the other. For a separate copy, write `names.ToList()` or `[..names]`. Arrays behave the same way.

Use an array when the number of items is fixed and a `List<T>` otherwise. Both work with `foreach`.
takeaways: Arrays have a fixed size; List<T> grows and shrinks
Items are numbered from 0; ^1 is the last item and a..b takes a range of items
Assigning a list to another variable shares it; it doesn't copy the items
pitfalls: Expecting var b = a; to copy a list: both variables now share one list.

quiz.q: List<int> a = [1]; var b = a; b.Add(2); What is a.Count?
quiz.explain: a and b refer to the same list, so the item added through b is visible through a.
Indexes start at 0, so a[1] is the second item, 20.

concepts.name: Classes and objects
concepts.summary: Define your own types with classes: fields for data, constructors for setup, methods for actions, and public/private access.
concepts.why: Classes are how C# programs describe the things they work with, such as accounts, orders or players, and what those things can do.
concepts.body:
So far data has lived in separate variables. Real programs describe things, such as a bank account with its holder's name and its balance, together with what you can do to them, such as deposit and withdraw. A **class** bundles that data and those actions into a new type of your own.

Think of a class as a blueprint and each thing built from it as an **object**. One `Account` class can produce thousands of accounts; each one is an **instance** of the class. You create one with `new`: `var acc = new Account("Ada");`.

What goes inside a class (its members):

- **Fields** are variables that belong to each object and hold its data, such as `_balance`.
- A **constructor** is setup code that runs when an object is created. It has the class's name and no return type, and its parameters are what `new Account(...)` must supply.
- Methods are the object's actions. Inside them, the object's own fields are available by name.
- A **static member** belongs to the class itself and is shared by all objects, like a count of how many accounts exist.

**Access modifiers** decide who may use a member. `public` means any code; `private` means only code inside this class, and is the default. Keep fields private and offer public methods, so the class can check every change: `Deposit` can refuse a negative amount.

When something is wrong, a method can stop with an error using `throw`, as `Deposit` does below; the exceptions lesson shows how to handle such errors.

Like lists, objects are reached through **references**: a variable holds a note saying where the object lives, so `var b = acc;` gives a second name to the same account. When no variable refers to an object any more, the **garbage collector**, part of the .NET runtime, frees the memory it used. You never delete objects yourself.

A shorter way to write a constructor is a primary constructor, with parameters right after the class name: `class Account(string owner) { ... }`.
takeaways: A class is a blueprint; new creates an object (an instance) from it
Fields hold each object's data, methods are its actions, the constructor sets it up
Keep fields private and change them through public methods that check the input
Variables hold references to objects; the garbage collector frees objects nobody uses
pitfalls: Making every field public, so any code can put the object into an invalid state.

quiz.q: What is the default access of a class member written without public or private?
quiz.explain: Members of classes are private unless you say otherwise.

quiz.q: var a = new Account("Ada"); var b = a; b.Deposit(10); Whose balance grows?
options: The single account that both a and b refer to
quiz.explain: Assigning an object to another variable copies the reference, so a and b reach the same account.

concepts.name: Properties and initialization
concepts.summary: Give classes a safe public face with properties: auto-properties, read-only and init-only ones, computed values and object initializers.
concepts.why: Properties are how C# classes normally expose their data, and many .NET libraries only look at properties.
concepts.body:
A field is just a variable inside an object. Often you want something that looks like a field to outside code but lets the class stay in control: readable but not changeable from outside, or tidied up when it's set. That is a **property**.

Outside code uses a property like a field: `p.Name = "Ada";` and `Console.WriteLine(p.Name);`. Inside, two small pieces of code decide what happens: `get` runs when someone reads it, `set` when someone assigns it.

The everyday form is the **auto-property**, `public string Name { get; set; }`, for which the compiler creates the hidden field that stores the value.

Variations:

- `{ get; private set; }`: everyone can read, only the class can change it.
- `{ get; init; }`: can be set only while the object is being created, then never again.
- `required` before the type makes the compiler insist that whoever creates the object sets it.
- A computed property works out its value each time it is read: `public int Age => DateTime.Today.Year - BirthYear;`.
- `= [];` after a property gives it a starting value, here an empty list.

An **object initializer** sets properties by name right after `new`: `new Person { Name = "Ada", BirthYear = 1815 }`. It is often clearer than a constructor with many parameters.

To check or clean a value as it is set, write the `set` part yourself. Inside it, `value` is the incoming value, and since C# 14 the word `field` means the hidden storage:

```csharp
public string Name { get; set => field = value.Trim(); }
```

Make public data properties rather than public fields. Many .NET libraries, for example the one that turns objects into JSON text, only look at properties.
takeaways: A property looks like a field from outside but runs get/set code inside
{ get; set; } is an auto-property: the compiler adds the hidden field
init and required make object initializers safe and readable
Use properties, not public fields, for public data
pitfalls: Writing a setter that assigns the property itself (set => Name = value): it calls itself over and over until the program crashes.

quiz.q: What does { get; init; } allow?
options: Setting it only during construction or an object initializer
Reading it only inside the class
quiz.explain: init accessors can be called during object creation, then the property is read-only.

concepts.name: Null and nullable types
concepts.summary: Handle missing values safely: null, string? and int?, the ?. and ?? operators, and the compiler's null warnings.
concepts.why: Using a missing value is the classic .NET crash; the compiler's null checks catch most of these before the program runs.
concepts.body:
Sometimes a value is simply missing: a user who hasn't entered a middle name, a search that found nobody. C# writes "no value here" as **null**.

Variables that hold references, such as strings, lists and objects, can be null: the note points nowhere. Using one as if something were there, like asking for `name.Length` when `name` is null, crashes the program with a `NullReferenceException`. It is the most common crash in .NET programs.

To catch this before the program runs, new projects switch on **nullable reference types**: the compiler tracks which variables may be null.

- `string` means "never null"; assigning `null` to it gets a warning.
- `string?`, with a question mark, means "may be null"; using it without checking first gets a warning.

The compiler follows your checks: after `if (name is null) return;` it knows `name` has a value. These are warnings, not errors, so read them: each one points at a possible crash.

Plain values such as `int`, `double` and `bool` can never be null. Add `?` when you need "maybe a number": `int? age = null;` (a **nullable** int). `age.HasValue` tells you whether there is one.

Helpful operators:

- `a?.Length` gives null instead of crashing when `a` is null.
- `x ?? fallback` uses `fallback` when `x` is null; `x ??= value` sets `x` only if it is null.
- `x is null` and `x is not null` are the clearest checks.
- `x!` tells the compiler "trust me, it's not null". It silences the warning but not the danger, so use it rarely.

To refuse a missing input at the start of a method, call `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(arg);`, which stops with a clear error.
takeaways: null means 'no value'; using it as if it were a value crashes the program
With nullable reference types on, string? may be null and string should not be
?. and ?? deal with null without crashing
Use ! rarely; check for null instead
pitfalls: Silencing every warning with ! instead of handling the null case.

quiz.q: What is the type of s?.Length when s is a string?
quiz.explain: ?. may produce null, so the int result becomes a nullable int?.

quiz.q: string? name = null; What does name ?? "guest" give?
quiz.explain: ?? uses the value on its right when the left side is null.

concepts.name: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Deal with errors while the program runs: throw and catch exceptions with try, catch and finally.
concepts.why: In .NET, errors arrive as exceptions; handling them in the right place keeps a program from crashing on bad input.
concepts.body:
Things go wrong while programs run: a file is missing, text that should be a number isn't, a value is out of range. The code that hits the problem **throws** an **exception**: an object describing what went wrong, such as a `FormatException` for text that isn't a number.

A thrown exception stops the current method at once. If the code that called that method doesn't deal with it, that code stops too, and so on back through every method waiting on another. That chain of "who called whom" is the **call stack**. If nothing deals with the exception, the program crashes and prints the message plus a **stack trace**: the list of those methods, which shows where the problem happened.

To deal with exceptions, put the risky code in a `try` block and add `catch` blocks; this is called **exception handling**:

```csharp
try { ... }
catch (FormatException ex) { ... }
catch (Exception ex) when (ex.Message.Contains("x")) { ... }
finally { ... }
```

- Each `catch` names the kind of exception it handles. They are tried in order, so put specific kinds before general ones; `Exception` matches every kind.
- `when (...)` adds a condition: that catch only applies when it is true.
- `finally` always runs, error or not; use it for clean-up.
- Inside a catch, `throw;` passes the same exception on unchanged. `throw ex;` would replace its stack trace, losing where the problem started.

You throw one yourself with `throw new ArgumentException("message")`. Pick a built-in kind that fits: `ArgumentException` or `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for a bad input, `InvalidOperationException` when the object isn't ready for this action.

Good habits: only catch exceptions you can actually do something about, and let the rest travel up to code that reports them. Never write an empty catch that hides the problem. When failure is normal, like a user typing letters where a number belongs, use `TryParse` instead of catching an exception.
takeaways: A thrown exception stops each method back up the call stack until a catch handles it
Put specific catch blocks before general ones; finally always runs
Use throw; to pass an exception on without losing its stack trace
Catch only what you can handle; never hide errors with an empty catch
pitfalls: Wrapping everything in catch (Exception) { } so real mistakes are silently hidden.

quiz.q: Why prefer throw; over throw ex; inside a catch block?
options: throw; keeps the original stack trace
throw; is only shorter to type
throw; also runs the finally block twice
quiz.explain: throw ex; restarts the stack trace at the catch block, hiding where the error really happened.

quiz.q: A method throws an exception and nothing catches it. What happens?
options: The program crashes and prints the message and stack trace
The compiler refuses to build the program
quiz.explain: An unhandled exception travels all the way up the call stack and ends the program.

concepts.name: Namespaces, projects and NuGet
concepts.summary: Organize code with namespaces and using directives, split it into projects, and add other people's libraries from NuGet.
concepts.why: Real programs span many files and use code written by others; this is how C# keeps all of that organized.
concepts.body:
As programs grow, code is split across many files and uses ready-made code written by others. C# keeps this organized with namespaces, projects and packages.

A **namespace** is a family name for related classes, so names don't clash: two pieces of code may both have a class called `Logger`, but `Serilog.Logger` and `Shop.Logger` are different. `List<T>` lives in the namespace `System.Collections.Generic`. Start each file with one line naming its namespace, such as `namespace Shop.Orders;`. Folders usually mirror namespaces.

To use a class from another namespace by its short name, add a **using directive** at the top of the file: `using System.Text;`. After it, `StringBuilder` works without `System.Text.` in front.

- New projects switch on **implicit usings**: common namespaces such as `System` and `System.Collections.Generic` are already available, which is why `Console` and `List<T>` just worked.
- `global using X;` in one file applies to every file in the project.

A project is one `.csproj` file plus its `.cs` files. Building it produces one **assembly**: a `.dll` file, or a program you can start. A larger app is several projects; one can use another's code after `dotnet add reference ../Lib/Lib.csproj`.

A **library** is ready-made code meant for other programs to use. Libraries are shared as **packages** on **NuGet**, .NET's online catalog. `dotnet add package Humanizer` adds the package to the `.csproj`, and the next build downloads it. Each package your project needs is one of its **dependencies**.

The access modifier `internal` makes a class visible only inside its own assembly, so a library can keep helper classes away from the projects that use it.
concepts.code:
<!-- Shop.csproj: the project file -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>                <!-- build a program you can start -->
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>  <!-- which .NET version -->
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>                 <!-- warn about possible nulls -->
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>     <!-- common namespaces everywhere -->
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- added by: dotnet add package Humanizer -->
    <PackageReference Include="Humanizer" Version="2.14.1" />
    <!-- added by: dotnet add reference ../Shop.Core/Shop.Core.csproj -->
    <ProjectReference Include="../Shop.Core/Shop.Core.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
takeaways: A namespace groups related classes; using directives let you write their short names
One .csproj project builds one assembly (a .dll or a program)
dotnet add package adds a NuGet package to the project
internal hides a class from code in other assemblies

quiz.q: What does internal mean on a class?
options: Visible only inside the same assembly (project)
quiz.explain: internal limits access to code compiled into the same assembly, regardless of namespace.

concepts.name: Structs, value and reference types
concepts.summary: Learn how value types (like structs) and reference types (like classes) differ in copying, equality, memory and boxing.
concepts.why: Many subtle bugs and performance issues come from not knowing whether a variable holds a value or a reference.
concepts.body:
Every C# type is one of two kinds, and the difference decides what happens when you copy a variable.

A **value type** keeps its data directly inside the variable. `int`, `double`, `bool`, `decimal`, `DateTime` and any **struct** you declare are value types. A struct is a small class-like type declared with `struct`: `struct Point { public int X; public int Y; }`. Copying a value-type variable copies the data, so changing the copy leaves the original alone.

A **reference type** keeps its data in an object stored elsewhere, in a memory area called the **heap**, and the variable holds only a reference to it. Classes, strings, arrays and lists are reference types. Copying the variable copies the reference: both variables then reach the same object.

The same rule applies to arguments: a method receives a copy of a struct, but a copy of the reference to a class object, so it can change that object.

Declare structs as `readonly struct` when you can, so their fields can't change after creation. Good candidates are small, value-like things: points, money amounts, date ranges.

Other differences:

- A struct always has a default value (all fields zero) and can't be null unless written `Point?`.
- `Equals` on two structs compares their fields (slowly, unless you write your own `Equals` or use a `record struct`); on two class objects it asks whether both references point at the same object.
- Struct local variables live in the method's own short-lived storage (the stack) or inside the object that contains them, so they give the garbage collector no extra work.

**Boxing** happens when a value type is stored in a variable of type `object`, which can hold anything: .NET creates a new heap object holding a copy. Unboxing copies it back out. Doing this millions of times in a loop costs time and memory. `List<int>` stores ints without boxing.

A common trap: changing a struct you got from a property or a list element changes a copy, not the stored value. The compiler rejects `list[0].X = 5` for that reason.
takeaways: Structs copy their data on assignment; classes copy references
Keep structs small and unchangeable (readonly struct)
Storing a value type in an object variable causes boxing: a copy on the heap
Changing a copy of a struct does not change the original
pitfalls: Making a large mutable struct and being surprised that changes 'disappear' on copies.

quiz.q: Which is a value type in C#?
quiz.explain: DateTime is a struct; strings, arrays and List<T> are reference types.

concepts.name: Inheritance and interfaces
concepts.summary: Reuse and abstract behavior with base classes, virtual/override, abstract classes and interfaces.
concepts.why: Interfaces make .NET code easy to test and to rearrange, and frameworks across .NET are built on inheritance.
concepts.body:
Often several classes share most of their code: a `Dog` and a `Cat` are both animals with a name. **Inheritance** lets one class build on another: `class Dog : Animal` means Dog gets all of Animal's members and can add its own. Animal is the **base class**; Dog is a **subclass** (also called a derived class). A C# class can inherit from only one base class, and its constructor passes values up with `: base(name)`.

A subclass can replace a method with its own version, but only if the base allows it: the base marks the method `virtual`, the subclass marks its version `override`. A variable of type `Animal` holding a `Dog` then runs Dog's version, so one call does the right thing for each type. That is **polymorphism**. Without `virtual`, a same-named method in the subclass only hides the base one (use the `new` keyword to say that's intended), and calls through an `Animal` variable still run Animal's version.

- An `abstract class` can't be created with `new`; it exists to be inherited, and its `abstract` members must be filled in by subclasses.
- `sealed` forbids inheriting from a class.
- `protected` members are visible to the class and its subclasses only.

An **interface** is a promise without code: `interface IShape { double Area(); }` says "anything that is an IShape has an Area method". A class can implement many interfaces but inherit only one class. Interface names start with `I` by convention. Interfaces may include default code, but most stay pure promises.

Prefer small interfaces, and classes that contain other objects (composition), over deep chains of inheritance. Code written against an interface such as `ILogger` works with any class that implements it, so tests can swap in a fake version. ASP.NET Core, Microsoft's web framework, builds on this: it hands each class the objects it asks for (**dependency injection**).

To check what an object really is while the program runs, use `is` (`if (shape is Circle c)`); but if you need many such checks, a virtual method is usually the better design.
takeaways: Single class inheritance, many interfaces
Methods are non-virtual unless marked virtual; derived classes override
abstract classes share code, interfaces define contracts
Depend on interfaces to make code swappable and testable
pitfalls: Forgetting virtual/override and getting the base implementation when calling through a base reference.

quiz.q: Animal has public void Speak() (not virtual). Dog declares new void Speak(). What does Animal a = new Dog(); a.Speak(); call?
options: It throws an error while running
quiz.explain: Without virtual, the variable's declared type (Animal) decides which method runs, so the base method runs.

concepts.name: Records
concepts.summary: Use record types for immutable data with value equality, with-expressions and positional syntax.
concepts.why: Records are the quickest way to describe plain data, such as messages, results and small values, with almost no code.
concepts.body:
A **record** is a class (or struct) designed for data. The positional form declares everything in one line:

```csharp
public record Person(string Name, int Age);
```

The compiler generates init-only properties, a constructor, a `Deconstruct` method (which lets you pull its values out: `var (name, age) = p;`), a readable `ToString()` (`Person { Name = Ada, Age = 36 }`), and **value equality**: two records are equal when their type and all properties are equal, so `==` compares contents rather than references.

Records encourage immutability. To "change" one, create a modified copy with a **with-expression**: `var older = p with { Age = 37 };`. The original is untouched. The copy is shallow: a property holding a reference, such as a list, points at the same list in both records.

Kinds of records:

- `record` (or `record class`) is a reference type.
- `record struct` is a value type with the same conveniences; `readonly record struct` makes it immutable.
- You can add methods, extra properties and validation in a body, and records support inheritance from other records.

Because equality compares contents, records work well as keys in dictionaries and sets (a later lesson) and are easy to compare in tests.

Use records for data that gets passed around: messages, the results of a calculation, the data a web service sends or receives, small values like an amount of money. Use ordinary classes for things with an identity that change over time, such as a customer whose address can change.
takeaways: Positional records generate properties, a constructor, ToString and Deconstruct
Records compare contents, classes compare references
with creates a modified shallow copy
record struct gives the same conveniences as a value type
pitfalls: Assuming with deep-copies collections inside the record; it only copies references.

quiz.q: For record R(List<int> Xs), var r2 = r1 with { }; r2.Xs.Add(1); what happens to r1.Xs?
options: It also contains 1 because the list is shared
quiz.explain: with performs a shallow copy, so both records reference the same list.

concepts.name: Generics
concepts.summary: Write type-safe reusable classes and methods with type parameters and constraints.
concepts.why: Generics power every collection and most libraries, and let you write one piece of code that works safely for many types.
concepts.body:
**Generics** let you write a class or method once and use it with any type, while the compiler still checks every use. `List<T>` is generic: `T` is a **type parameter**, a placeholder filled in when you write `List<int>` or `List<string>`. `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` (a later lesson) has two.

Generic method: `static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T> => a.CompareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b;`. You usually don't write the type yourself: from `Max(3, 7)` the compiler works out that `T` is `int` (**type inference**).

Generic class: `class Box<T> { public T Value { get; set; } }`, used as `new Box<string>()`.

**Constraints** (written with `where`) say what `T` must support, so you can call those members:

- `where T : class` / `where T : struct` (reference or value type), `where T : notnull`.
- `where T : new()` requires a constructor with no parameters.
- `where T : SomeBase` or `where T : IComparable<T>` for a base class or interface.
- `where T : INumber<T>` (generic math, .NET 7+) lets you use `+` and `T.Zero` on any numeric type.

Unlike Java's generics, .NET keeps the real type while the program runs: `List<int>` and `List<string>` are different types, `typeof(T)` tells you which `T` you got, and value types like `int` are stored directly, without boxing.

`default(T)` (or just `default`) gives null for reference types and zero for value types. Prefer generics over `object` parameters: the compiler keeps checking your types, and you avoid converting values back by hand.
takeaways: Type parameters give reuse without conversions or boxing
Constraints (where T : ...) unlock members you can call on T
The compiler usually infers the type for generic methods
.NET keeps generic types at runtime: typeof(T) works

quiz.q: Why does Max<T>(T a, T b) need where T : IComparable<T> to call a.CompareTo(b)?
options: It doesn't; all types have CompareTo
Constraints make the method run faster
Without the constraint the compiler only knows T has the members every object has
Because generic types are forgotten while the program runs
quiz.explain: An unconstrained T only offers the basic members of object; the constraint guarantees CompareTo exists.

concepts.name: Dictionaries and sets
concepts.summary: Look up values by key with Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and keep unique items with HashSet<T>.
concepts.why: Dictionaries and sets turn slow searches through a list into near-instant lookups, and they appear in most real code.
concepts.body:
A **dictionary** stores values under keys, like a phone book: look up "Ada" and get her number. `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` finds a key almost instantly however many entries it holds (written O(1)), while searching a list gets slower as the list grows. Create one with `new() { ["a"] = 1 }` and use:

- `dict[key] = value` adds or overwrites.
- `dict[key]` reads, but throws `KeyNotFoundException` if missing.
- `TryGetValue(key, out var v)` reads safely; `ContainsKey`, `Remove`, `Count`.
- `GetValueOrDefault(key, fallback)` for a default.
- `foreach (var (key, value) in dict)` iterates pairs (order is not guaranteed).

`HashSet<T>` holds unique items: `Add` returns false when the item is already present, `Contains` is just as fast, and `UnionWith`, `IntersectWith` and `ExceptWith` combine two sets.

Both work by **hashing**: each key's `GetHashCode` method turns it into a number that says where to look, and `Equals` confirms the match. Strings, numbers and records work without extra effort; for your own classes, override both consistently, or two objects with the same contents count as different keys. Never mutate an object while it is a key.

Pass a comparer to change equality, e.g. `new Dictionary<string, int>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`.

Other useful types: `SortedDictionary` (keeps keys in order, slightly slower lookups), `Queue<T>` (first in, first out), `Stack<T>` (last in, first out), `PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>`, and `FrozenDictionary` for lookup tables built once and then only read. When several parts of a program running at the same time share one dictionary, use `ConcurrentDictionary`.
takeaways: Dictionary lookups stay fast however many entries there are
Use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault instead of catching KeyNotFoundException
HashSet.Add returns false for duplicates
Keys need matching Equals and GetHashCode
pitfalls: Using a mutable class without Equals/GetHashCode as a key and expecting equal contents to match.

quiz.q: What happens when you read dict["missing"] on a Dictionary<string,int>?
quiz.explain: The indexer getter throws for missing keys; use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault instead.

concepts.name: Delegates, lambdas and events
concepts.summary: Pass behavior as values with Func, Action and lambda expressions, and publish notifications with events.
concepts.why: Lambdas are everywhere in modern C#: in LINQ queries, web app setup, and anywhere code says 'run this when...'.
concepts.body:
A **delegate** is a type for variables that hold a method, so behavior can be stored, passed to another method and called later. You rarely declare your own; the built-in generic delegates cover most needs:

- `Func<T1, ..., TResult>` takes arguments and returns a value: `Func<int, int> square`.
- `Action<T1, ...>` returns nothing.
- `Predicate<T>` is an older name for `Func<T, bool>`.

A **lambda** writes a small method right where it is used, without a name: `x => x * x` means "take x, give back x times x". Other forms: `(a, b) => a + b`, or a block `x => { var y = x * 2; return y; }`. Since C# 10, `var add = (int a, int b) => a + b;` works on its own, and since C# 12 lambdas can have default parameter values.

A lambda can use variables from the code around it; it then **captures** them and is called a **closure**. It captures the variable itself, not a snapshot of its value, so later changes are visible. Write `static x => ...` to forbid capturing, which avoids hidden extra objects.

A method's name on its own also works as a delegate: `names.ForEach(Console.WriteLine);`.

An **event** lets other code ask to be told when something happens, like signing up for a doorbell. Outside code subscribes with `+=` and unsubscribes with `-=`; only the owning class can raise it. The convention is `event EventHandler<TArgs>? Changed;`, raised with `Changed?.Invoke(this, args)`. A long-lived object keeps every subscriber alive while it is subscribed, so forgetting `-=` can make memory use grow without end: a **memory leak**.
takeaways: Func returns a value, Action does not
Lambdas capture variables, not snapshots of their values
Outside code can subscribe to an event with += but not raise it
Unsubscribe from long-lived events to avoid memory leaks
pitfalls: Capturing a loop variable of a for loop in lambdas and seeing its final value in all of them.

quiz.q: int x = 1; Func<int> f = () => x; x = 5; What does f() return?
quiz.explain: The lambda captures the variable x itself, so it sees the latest value 5.

concepts.name: LINQ
concepts.summary: Query and transform collections with LINQ methods like Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy and ToList.
concepts.why: LINQ is the usual way to work with data in C#, from lists in memory to databases.
concepts.body:
**LINQ** (Language Integrated Query) is a set of methods, from the `System.Linq` namespace, that work on any sequence you can `foreach` over: anything that implements the interface `IEnumerable<T>`, such as arrays and lists. Each method takes a lambda saying what to do, and you chain them into a **pipeline** where each step feeds the next:

- `Where(pred)` keeps the items for which the lambda returns true; `Select(f)` turns each item into something else; `SelectMany` flattens a list of lists.
- `OrderBy`, `ThenBy`, `OrderByDescending` sort.
- `GroupBy(keySelector)` produces groups, each with a `Key`.
- `First`, `FirstOrDefault`, `Single`, `Any`, `All`, `Count`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Min`, `Max`, `MaxBy`.
- `Distinct`, `Take`, `Skip`, `Chunk`, `Zip`, `Join`, `ToDictionary`, `ToLookup`.
- .NET 9 added `CountBy` and `AggregateBy`.

Most of these methods are **lazy**: `Where` and `Select` only describe the work. It actually runs when you loop over the result or call a method that needs real results, such as `ToList()`, `ToArray()`, `Count()` or `First()`. A query looped over twice runs twice, so call `ToList()` once if you reuse the results or the source is slow.

There is also query syntax (`from p in people where p.Age > 30 select p.Name`), which compiles to the same method calls; the method style is more common.

Entity Framework Core, .NET's main database library, accepts the same methods and translates them into SQL, the language databases understand, instead of running them in memory. So LINQ skills carry over to working with databases.

`First` throws if nothing matches; `FirstOrDefault` returns the type's default value (null, or 0 for numbers). `Single` also throws if more than one item matches.
takeaways: Chain Where, Select, OrderBy and GroupBy into readable pipelines
Most LINQ methods are lazy: nothing runs until you loop or call ToList()
Call ToList() once when you reuse results
Database libraries translate the same methods into SQL
pitfalls: Looping over a lazy query several times, re-running expensive work each time.

quiz.q: var q = list.Where(x => x > 2); list.Add(10); How many items does q.Count() see for list = [1, 3]?
quiz.explain: Where is deferred, so the query runs at Count() time and sees both 3 and the newly added 10.

concepts.name: Pattern matching and switch expressions
concepts.summary: Test shapes of data with type, property, relational, list and logical patterns in is and switch expressions.
concepts.why: Patterns replace long if/else chains and type conversions with short decisions the compiler checks for you.
concepts.body:
**Pattern matching** tests a value against a shape and can extract parts of it. It works with `is` and with **switch expressions**.

```csharp
var label = shape switch { Circle c => ..., _ => "?" };
```

Pattern kinds:

- **Type pattern**: `obj is string s` checks whether `obj` holds a string and, if so, gives it to you as the string variable `s`, in one step.
- **Constant**: `x is null`, `status is "ok"`.
- **Relational**: `< 0`, `>= 18`; combine with `and`, `or`, `not`: `n is > 0 and < 10`.
- **Property pattern**: `order is { Status: "paid", Total: > 100 }`, nested as deep as you like.
- **Positional pattern** on types with `Deconstruct` (records): `Point(0, 0)`.
- **List patterns** (C# 11): `[1, .., var last]`, `[]`, `[_, _]`.
- **Discard** `_` matches anything; `var x` matches and captures.

A switch expression is an expression that must produce a value; arms are tried top to bottom and `_` is the fallback. The compiler warns when the arms (the `pattern => result` lines) don't cover every possible input, and reports an error when an arm can never be reached because an earlier one already catches everything it would. That is especially useful with enums, types that have a fixed list of named values.

Use switch expressions for mapping inputs to results: price rules, turning codes into messages, deciding the next step. Keep complex logic in methods and patterns for the decision itself.
concepts.code:
static string Describe(object o) => o switch
{
    null => "null",
    int n when n < 0 => "negative int",
    int n and > 100 => $"big int {n}",
    int => "small int",
    string { Length: 0 } => "empty string",
    string s => $"string '{s}'",
    Order { Status: "paid", Total: > 100 } => "big paid order",
    Order { Items: [var only] } => $"order of one {only}",
    Order { Items: [var first, ..] } => $"order starting with {first}",
    _ => "something else",
};

Console.WriteLine(Describe(250));       // big int 250
Console.WriteLine(Describe(-5));        // negative int
Console.WriteLine(Describe(""));        // empty string
Console.WriteLine(Describe(new Order("paid", 500m, ["tv"])));    // big paid order
Console.WriteLine(Describe(new Order("new", 5m, ["pen"])));      // order of one pen
Console.WriteLine(Describe(new Order("new", 9m, ["a", "b"])));   // order starting with a
Console.WriteLine(Describe(3.5));       // something else

record Order(string Status, decimal Total, string[] Items);
takeaways: obj is T t checks the type and gives you a typed variable in one step
Property, relational and list patterns describe the shape of data
Switch expressions return a value; arms are checked top to bottom
The compiler flags missing arms and arms that can never match
pitfalls: Putting a broad arm (like string s) before a more specific one, which makes the latter unreachable.

quiz.q: What does 7 is > 0 and < 5 evaluate to?
quiz.explain: 7 is greater than 0 but not less than 5, so the combined pattern fails.

concepts.name: async and await
concepts.summary: Wait for slow work such as downloads without blocking, using Task, async methods and await, and run several operations at once.
concepts.why: Downloads, files and databases in .NET are all used this way, and a web server only handles many users at once if you get it right.
concepts.body:
Many operations spend most of their time waiting: downloading a web page, reading a file, asking another computer for data. This waiting on the outside world is called **I/O** (input/output). A **thread** is the worker inside your program that carries out statements one after another; while it just waits, it can do nothing else. A program serving thousands of users can't afford thousands of idle, waiting threads.

**Asynchronous** code lets the thread do other work while waiting. In .NET, a `Task` represents an operation that will finish later; `Task<T>` will also produce a value of type `T`. Inside a method marked `async`, `await task` pauses *this method* until the task finishes, without holding on to the thread, and then continues where it left off. Meanwhile the method has already handed its caller a `Task`, which the caller can await in turn.

```csharp
async Task<string> LoadAsync(string url) => await http.GetStringAsync(url);
```

Rules of thumb:

- Name async methods with an `Async` ending and return `Task` or `Task<T>` (or `ValueTask<T>`, an Expert topic). Use `async void` only for event handlers: nobody can await it, and an exception from it crashes the program.
- Go async all the way up. Waiting on a task with `.Result` or `.Wait()` blocks the thread and, in desktop apps, can freeze the program for good: a **deadlock**, two things each waiting for the other.
- To run independent operations at the same time, start them all first, then await them together: `await Task.WhenAll(t1, t2)`. Awaiting one after the other runs them in sequence.
- `await Task.Delay(ms)` waits without blocking, unlike `Thread.Sleep`.
- An exception thrown inside an async method is stored in its task and thrown again at the `await`, so ordinary `try`/`catch` works.
- Pass a `CancellationToken` through so the work can be stopped early (an Advanced lesson).

Async helps while you're waiting, not when the processor is busy calculating. For heavy calculations, `Task.Run` hands the work to a background thread from .NET's **thread pool**, a set of ready-made worker threads.

In `Program.cs` you can use `await` directly.
takeaways: await pauses the method without blocking the thread
Start tasks first, then await Task.WhenAll to run them at the same time
Avoid `.Result`, `.Wait()` and `async void`
Exceptions come out at the await
pitfalls: Calling an async method without awaiting it, so errors are lost and work may not finish.

quiz.q: Two independent 1-second async calls are awaited one after the other. Roughly how long does it take?
quiz.explain: Each await waits for its call to finish before the next starts; use Task.WhenAll to overlap them.

concepts.name: IDisposable and using
concepts.summary: Release files, connections and other resources promptly and reliably with IDisposable and using declarations.
concepts.why: Files and connections that are never released pile up and can bring a service down; the garbage collector won't release them in time.
concepts.body:
The garbage collector frees memory, but only eventually, and it knows nothing about the other things a program takes from the operating system: open files, network connections, database connections. These must be handed back promptly, or the system runs out of them. Types that hold such resources implement the `IDisposable` interface, whose `Dispose()` method releases them right away.

The `using` statement guarantees `Dispose` is called, even if an exception is thrown:

```csharp
using (var reader = new StreamReader(path)) { ... }
```

The more common **using declaration** disposes at the end of the surrounding block (the enclosing braces): `using var conn = new SqlConnection(cs);`. Multiple declarations are disposed in reverse order.

For resources released asynchronously (see the async lesson) there is `IAsyncDisposable` with `DisposeAsync()`, used with `await using`.

Guidelines:

- If you create a disposable object and own it, dispose it. If it was given to you (for example by dependency injection), whoever created it disposes it.
- Some types are meant to live long: `HttpClient`, used for web requests, should be reused (or created via `IHttpClientFactory`), not created and disposed for every request.
- Implementing `IDisposable` in your own class is needed when it owns other disposables: call their `Dispose` from yours. The full "dispose pattern", with a finalizer (a method the garbage collector calls before freeing an object), is only needed when your class directly holds raw handles from the operating system, and the built-in `SafeHandle` class usually does that job for you.
- After disposal, objects typically throw `ObjectDisposedException` when used.
takeaways: IDisposable releases things other than memory, such as files and connections, right away
using var disposes at the end of the block, even when an exception is thrown
await using for IAsyncDisposable
Dispose what you own; reuse HttpClient instead of disposing it per call
pitfalls: Creating a new HttpClient for every web request, which can run the machine out of network connections under load.

quiz.q: When is a using var x = ... declaration disposed?
options: At the end of the enclosing block, even if an exception is thrown
Never, unless Dispose is called manually
quiz.explain: A using declaration calls Dispose when control leaves the enclosing scope by any route.

concepts.name: Unit testing with xUnit
concepts.summary: Write and run automated tests with xUnit, Fact and Theory attributes, and dotnet test.
concepts.why: Tests let you change and tidy code with confidence, and every professional .NET codebase has them.
concepts.body:
A **unit test** is a small piece of code that calls one piece of your code and checks the result automatically. .NET has three popular test frameworks, libraries for writing and running tests: **xUnit**, NUnit and MSTest. They work the same way: a separate test project uses the code being tested, and `dotnet test` finds and runs the tests.

```bash
dotnet new xunit -o Calc.Tests
dotnet add Calc.Tests reference Calc
dotnet test
```

In xUnit:

- `[Fact]` marks a test method with no parameters. Square-bracket labels like this are **attributes**: notes attached to code that tools, here the test runner, read.
- `[Theory]` with `[InlineData(...)]` runs the same test for several inputs.
- An **assertion** checks a result and fails the test if it's wrong: `Assert.Equal(expected, actual)`, `Assert.True`, `Assert.Null`, `Assert.Contains`. `Assert.Throws<T>(() => ...)` checks that the code inside, written as a small method in place (a lambda), throws an exception of type `T`.
- A new object of the test class is created for each test, so the constructor is per-test setup. Expensive setup can be shared with class fixtures (`IClassFixture<T>`).

Follow **Arrange, Act, Assert**: set up the inputs, call the method, check the result. Name tests after the behavior they check (`Withdraw_MoreThanBalance_Throws`).

To test code without a real database or network, write it against interfaces and pass in fake versions; libraries such as NSubstitute or Moq create these fakes (**mocks**) for you. Async methods are tested by making the test method `async Task`.

Run some of the tests with `dotnet test --filter "FullyQualifiedName~Calc"`, and measure which lines your tests ran (code coverage) with `--collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"`.
takeaways: Tests live in a separate project; dotnet test runs them
[Fact] for one scenario, [Theory] + [InlineData] for a table of inputs
xUnit creates a new test class object for each test
Write code against interfaces so tests can pass in fakes
pitfalls: Tests that depend on each other's leftover data or on the order they run in.

quiz.q: In xUnit, how do you run one test method with several input sets?
options: Copy the method for each input
quiz.explain: A Theory is executed once per InlineData row, and each row is reported as its own test.

concepts.name: Iterators and yield return
concepts.summary: Produce lazy sequences with yield return, and understand IEnumerable, IEnumerator and lazy evaluation.
concepts.why: Iterators are how LINQ and streaming code process large or infinite data without loading it all.
concepts.body:
Anything you can `foreach` over implements `IEnumerable<T>`, which hands out an `IEnumerator<T>` with `MoveNext()` and `Current`. Writing enumerators by hand is tedious; **iterator methods** let the compiler do it.

A method returning `IEnumerable<T>` that contains `yield return` becomes an iterator. The compiler turns it into a **state machine**, an object that remembers where the method paused: nothing runs when you call the method; each `MoveNext()` runs the body until the next `yield return`, hands out that value and pauses. `yield break` ends the sequence.

Consequences:

- Sequences are **lazy** and can be infinite: `Naturals().Take(5)` is fine.
- Each enumeration restarts the method from the beginning.
- Argument checks in an iterator run only on the first `MoveNext()`, not at the call. To check right away, put the checks in a normal method that then returns the result of a separate iterator method.
- `finally` blocks inside iterators run when the loop over them ends, even when a `foreach` stops early with `break`.

`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is the async counterpart: an `async` method with `yield return` produces items consumed with `await foreach`. It's ideal for database rows or web results that arrive a page at a time.

This is exactly how LINQ's `Where` and `Select` are implemented, which is why they are lazy.
takeaways: yield return turns a method into a lazy iterator
Nothing runs until you loop over it; each loop starts it again
Check arguments right away in a normal wrapper method
IAsyncEnumerable + await foreach handle data that arrives asynchronously
pitfalls: Expecting an exception from argument checks at call time in an iterator method.

quiz.q: An iterator method throws ArgumentNullException at its first line. When is it thrown for var seq = Get(null);?
options: When the sequence is first enumerated
quiz.explain: Iterator bodies don't run until MoveNext is called, so the check is deferred.

concepts.name: Extension methods and members
concepts.summary: Add methods and properties to existing types with extension methods and C# 14 extension blocks.
concepts.why: Extensions are how LINQ, ASP.NET Core app setup (AddX/UseX) and chainable 'fluent' APIs are built.
concepts.body:
An **extension method** is a static method in a static class whose first parameter has the `this` modifier. It can be called as if it were an instance method of that type:

```csharp
public static class StringExtensions
{
    public static bool IsBlank(this string? s) => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s);
}
// "  ".IsBlank()
```

It's only syntax: the compiler rewrites the call to `StringExtensions.IsBlank("  ")`. Extensions can only access public members, are found only when their namespace is imported, and a method the type itself has with the same name and parameters always wins. The value before the dot (the receiver) is just the first argument, so an extension can even be called on null.

**C# 14 extension blocks** generalize this. Inside a static class, `extension(Type receiver) { ... }` can declare extension methods, extension **properties**, and static extension members on the type itself:

```csharp
extension(string s) { public bool IsBlank => string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(s); }
```

Typical uses:

- Fluent setup, where calls chain one after another, as in ASP.NET Core apps: `builder.Services.AddMyFeature()`, `app.UseMyMiddleware()`.
- Helpers on interfaces, giving every implementer shared behavior, as LINQ does for `IEnumerable<T>`.
- Domain helpers on types you don't own.

Don't overuse them: extensions on `object` or very common types clutter the suggestions your editor shows everywhere, and behavior that needs private state belongs in the type itself.
takeaways: Extension methods are static methods called as if they belonged to the type
They are visible only where their namespace is imported
A type's own method wins over an extension with the same name and parameters
C# 14 extension blocks add extension properties and static members
pitfalls: Writing extensions that need private state of the type; they can't access it.

quiz.q: How is "x".IsBlank() compiled when IsBlank is an extension method?
options: As a virtual call on string
quiz.explain: Extension method calls are rewritten by the compiler into ordinary static method calls.

concepts.name: Cancellation and parallelism
concepts.summary: Stop async work with CancellationToken, limit how much runs at once, and spread heavy calculations over processor cores.
concepts.why: Real services must stop work promptly when a user gives up or a time limit passes, and should use every processor core well.
concepts.body:
**Cancellation** in .NET is cooperative: nothing is forcibly stopped; code checks whether it has been asked to stop. A `CancellationTokenSource` creates a `CancellationToken`, which you pass down through every async method. Library methods (`HttpClient`, Entity Framework Core, `Task.Delay`) watch it and throw `OperationCanceledException` when it fires; your own loops call `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`. Set a time limit (a **timeout**) with `new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))` or `CancelAfter`, and combine sources with `CreateLinkedTokenSource`. In ASP.NET Core, `HttpContext.RequestAborted` fires when the user's browser disconnects.

Limiting how much runs at once:

- `Task.WhenAll` over a thousand tasks starts them all at once. To cap that, use `Parallel.ForEachAsync(items, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4 }, async (item, ct) => ...)` or a `SemaphoreSlim`.
- `Task.WhenAny` waits for the first task to finish: useful for time limits, or for asking two servers and taking the faster answer.

Heavy calculations are **CPU-bound**: limited by processor speed rather than by waiting. For them use `Parallel.For`/`Parallel.ForEach` or PLINQ (`.AsParallel()`), which split the items across thread pool threads so several processor cores work at once.

Data that several threads change then needs protection, or two threads may change it at the same moment and one change gets lost (a **race condition**). Use `lock`, `Interlocked.Increment`, or the thread-safe collections in `System.Collections.Concurrent`.

`System.Threading.Channels` provides fast async queues between producers (code that creates items) and consumers (code that processes them): producers call `WriteAsync`, consumers `await foreach (var x in reader.ReadAllAsync(ct))`. A bounded channel holds only a limited number of items, so a fast producer has to wait for the consumer to catch up: **backpressure**.

Treat `OperationCanceledException` as a normal outcome, not an error, when your own token was canceled.
takeaways: Pass a CancellationToken through every async call chain
Cap how much runs at once with Parallel.ForEachAsync or SemaphoreSlim
Protect data shared between threads with Interlocked, lock or concurrent collections
Channels give async producer/consumer queues with backpressure
pitfalls: Accepting a CancellationToken parameter but never passing it to the calls that do the waiting.

quiz.q: How does cancellation with a CancellationToken work in .NET?
options: The runtime aborts the thread running the task
Code must observe the token; awaited APIs throw OperationCanceledException
quiz.explain: Cancellation is cooperative: methods check the token and throw OperationCanceledException.
